paragraphs: A hypersonic glide vehicle looks unlike a conventional missile because it has to fly rather than merely arc: a wedge-shaped body that generates lift at speed, control surfaces at the rear and a blunted nose sized to survive the heat of the descent. Presented in black, those planform edges read clearly, which is what a defence graphic needs.
The mesh carries 39,234 polygons with mixed UV layout, and the geometry is spent on the body chines and the control surfaces where the shape has to be exact.

At $59 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits defence and geopolitical visualisation, news and documentary graphics, strategic analysis material, education and games. Real-world scale is kept, so it seats correctly on a launch vehicle. On sale since 2026.

An AC75 is a monohull that does not touch the water once it is up to speed. The hull is a canoe-shaped shell with two enormous foil arms swinging out from the sides, one lowered to lift the boat and one raised as ballast. That asymmetry in flight is the image everyone knows from the America's Cup, and the model carries the foil arms and the hull profile that produce it.

The mesh is efficient at 43,460 polygons and 44,077 vertices in quads and tris. The UVs overlap, which is a fair economy on a symmetrical racing hull, and the StemCell build means it works in a real-time engine.
At $59 it suits sailing and regatta broadcast graphics, sports advertising, marine and yacht design presentation, coastal scenes and games. On sale since 2026.

The RPG-7 is among the most recognisable weapons in the world: a smoothbore tube with a wooden heat guard, a pistol grip below and a shaped-charge grenade sticking out of the muzzle with its fins folded. That protruding round is what makes the silhouette unmistakable, and any model that omits it stops being an RPG.
The mesh is 57,716 polygons and 31,901 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the detail concentrated in the sight rail, the grip assembly and the grenade nose.

At $59 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits defence and conflict visualisation, news and documentary graphics, film and television armouries, games and training material. Real-world scale is kept, so it fits a character rig correctly. On sale since 2024.

An urchin served as food is cut open across the top and presented in its own shell, with the roe sitting inside in five orange-yellow lobes arranged like a star. That arrangement is the whole visual of uni, and it cannot be improvised - a shell with something yellow in it looks wrong to anyone who has eaten one.
The mesh is 25,594 polygons and 27,392 vertices in quads and tris with mixed UV layout, with the density in the spines and the roe surface where the texture has to read as wet and soft.

At $59 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits seafood and restaurant visualisation, menu and food photography work, culinary advertising, marine biology material and games. On sale since 2026.

A beam tester is a tall box on a wheeled column that rolls up to a car's headlight and shows whether the beam points where regulations say it should. Every MOT bay and service workshop has one, and its shape is unmistakable: a mirror box with a lens on the front, a levelling sight on top and a heavy base on castors.
The mesh is 56,278 polygons and 58,175 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the detail in the column, the adjustment mechanism and the front lens housing.

A rigged build sits on this page at the same $59 for when the box has to be raised or rotated. Aimed at automotive workshop and service visualisation, garage equipment marketing, technical and training material, and games. On sale since 2021.

Counter-drone systems are mostly antennas, and that is what makes them interesting to model: a detection radar, a set of directional jammers, an optical tracker and the mast that carries them, all packaged to be mounted on a vehicle and set up quickly. This build is the system itself, and the density here is exceptional.

At 4,828,176 polygons and 2,444,600 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, this is one of the heaviest assets in the catalogue relative to its physical size. Every antenna element and mounting bracket is geometry, which is what lets a close camera examine the array rather than only pass over it.

Two other builds sit on this page: the system mounted on an Oshkosh M-ATV at $169, and a rigged version of that vehicle at $199. Aimed at defence visualisation, news graphics, counter-UAS presentation and training material. On sale since 2022.

JASSM is a stealthy cruise missile, and this build shows it in the flight configuration: wings deployed, tail fins out, engine inlet open. On the pylon the missile is a folded slab; in flight it becomes a small aircraft, and those are two visually different objects. This is the one that belongs in a strike graphic.

The mesh is deliberately light at 10,352 polygons and 10,340 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs. Cruise missiles appear in numbers in a salvo graphic, and weight matters more here than surface complexity.

At $49 it suits defence visualisation, news and documentary graphics, military aviation renders, training material and games. Real-world scale is kept, so it sits correctly relative to a launching aircraft. On sale since 2021.

The AKS-74 is the folding-stock version of the small calibre Kalashnikov, and the details that identify it are specific: the distinctive muzzle brake, the smooth magazine curve, the side-folding skeleton stock and the gas block angle. A generic Kalashnikov shape with a different magazine will not pass with anyone who knows the family.

The mesh is 46,721 polygons and 48,335 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 12 texture maps - 8 at 4096x4096 and 4 at 2048x2048. That budget carries the parkerised metal, the polymer furniture and the wear at the handling points.

At $49 it suits military and conflict visualisation, film and television armouries, games, documentary work and training material. Real-world scale is kept, so it fits a character rig correctly. On sale since 2016.

The TOW is a wire-guided anti-tank missile, which means it is nearly always seen as a launch tube rather than as a bare round. These are the missiles in their sealed tubes, which is the form they appear in on a vehicle mount, a tripod or a reload rack, and that is what a defence render usually needs.

The mesh is 77,518 polygons and 77,799 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 7 texture maps at 4096x4096, carrying the stencilling and the end cap detail that identify the round.

At $49 it suits defence visualisation, news and documentary graphics, military training material, film and television, and games. Real-world scale is kept, so the tubes seat correctly in a launcher. On sale since 2017.

The paired masks are one of the oldest visual shorthands there is, and the pairing is the point: one mouth turned up, one turned down, otherwise near-identical. That symmetry means any asymmetry in the modelling is immediately visible, since the eye compares the two faces directly.

The meshes are light at 4,953 polygons and 4,942 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, which suits objects whose interest lies in silhouette and material rather than in surface complexity.

At $49 and built to CheckMate specification, they suit theatre and performing arts material, event and festival design, carnival and masquerade visualisation, decorative interiors, print and games. On sale since 2025.

A twin tone horn set is two snail-shaped horns pitched slightly apart, wired to sound together, which is what gives a car its two-note note rather than a flat blare. Each horn is a spiral casing with a mounting bracket and a spade terminal, and the pair are usually mounted behind the grille where nobody sees them until a bonnet is open.

The mesh is light at 10,095 polygons and 10,012 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 12 texture maps at 2048x2048 carrying the casing paint, the labelling and the terminal detail.

At $49 and built to StemCell specification, it suits automotive parts and accessory marketing, engine bay visualisation, workshop and service scenes, technical catalogues and games. On sale since 2021.

A lamb is not a small sheep, and getting that difference right is the whole task. The legs are disproportionately long, the fleece is short and tight rather than heavy, the head is large relative to the body and the ears sit out sideways. Scale down an adult sheep and you get something that reads as wrong without a viewer being able to say why.
The mesh is light at 13,398 polygons and 13,595 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 3 texture maps at 4096x4096 carrying the fleece and the face detail.

A rigged build sits on this page at $79 for animation. The static model at $49 covers farming and agriculture visualisation, food and dairy advertising, children's and educational material, pastoral scenes, seasonal work and games. Built to StemCell specification, on sale since 2016.

A broom and dustpan are the least glamorous objects in any interior render and among the most useful, because they say a space is used and maintained rather than staged. The set works as a pair: the pan clips onto the broom handle for storage, which is why both share a design language and why showing one without the other looks incomplete.

The meshes are light at 6,964 polygons and 5,056 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ship with 4 texture maps at 4096x4096. Almost all the realism is in those maps: the bristle bunching and the moulded plastic finish.
At $49 it suits interior and facility visualisation, cleaning and janitorial industry presentation, retail and catalogue renders, film and television set dressing, and games. On sale since 2015.

An LNG trailer is a vacuum-insulated pressure vessel on wheels, and the engineering is on display: a long cylindrical tank with domed ends, a valve and manifold cabinet at the rear, heavy frame rails and a rounded profile that has nothing in common with a dry bulk tanker. The insulation is why the tank has no visible ribs and why the shell is so smooth.

The mesh is 251,874 polygons and 252,096 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 12 texture maps - 11 at 4096x4096 and one at 2048x2048, carrying the hazard placards and the polished tank finish.

Three other builds sit on this page, including a Kenworth W990 with the trailer at $149 and rigged versions at $59. Aimed at energy and logistics visualisation, gas industry marketing, highway scenes and games. On sale since 2019.
